anchor.quote: G(D_v g_1, \dots, D_v g_t) = D_v\, G(g_1, \dots, g_t).
anchor.note: The page uses g_1 as an input array of the gate, but never says what the indexed symbol g_1 denotes; the only listed binding is for the unindexed g.

anchor.quote: G(D_v g_1, \dots, D_v g_t) = D_v\, G(g_1, \dots, g_t).
anchor.note: The page uses g_t as the last input array of the gate, but never says what the indexed symbol g_t denotes.
g_2 first appears in the worked example as an input to pointwise addition; the example gives its value but nothing says what g_2 denotes.

gaps.term: identity for a pointwise linear gate
gaps.quote: The reason for the shared frame is the identity that a pointwise linear gate satisfies.
gaps.note: The page states the identity G(D_v g_1, ..., D_v g_t) = D_v G(g_1, ..., g_t) for all arrays but gives no derivation; the only check is one two-entry example. The reader must supply the argument from linearity of D_v and the form of the gate.

gaps.quote: The identity needs all $t$ incidences of the gate to use the same $D_v$
gaps.note: The page claims that with different frames no single operator would move the result back, but gives no calculation or argument for this failure.

gaps.quote: the frame of the gate is shared by all of them
gaps.note: Frames are defined on vertices, and the page never says what the frame of a gate is or that a gate has a frame of its own.

gaps.quote: A wire carries its frame change along its length
gaps.note: The page asserts that a wire carries a frame change along its length, and that the frame of an incidence is therefore the gate frame on that side. It does not explain how or why a wire does this.
